 S1. Material synthesis, characterization techniques, and experimental procedures

Figure  S1.  Schematic  representation  of  the  synthesis,  characterization,  and  experimental 

methodology.

 S2. Instrumentation and LC-MS/MS Conditions

The UPLC-MS/MS system (Acquity H-Class, Waters, Milford, MA, USA), equipped with a 

triple  quadrupole  mass  detector  (Xevo-TQD,  Waters,  Milford,  MA,  USA)  and  utilizing 

electrospray  ionization  (ESI),  was  employed  for  both  qualitative  and  quantitative  pesticide 

analysis. It was also used to determine the degradation rates of methiocarb (MTC), carbofuran 

(CBF), carbaryl (CBR), and dimethoate (DMT) at various reaction intervals (0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 

and 25 minutes).

Separation was carried out on an Acquity UPLC BEH C18 column (130 Å, 1.7 µm, 2.1 mm × 

100 mm; Waters Corporation, Milford, MA, USA). The mobile phase was composed of:

Channel B: 5 mM ammonium formate in 0.1% formic acid methanol.

Channel D: 5 mM ammonium formate in 0.1% formic acid water.

The  flow  rate  was  consistently  maintained  at  0.25  mL/min  throughout  the  analysis.  The 

gradient elution program followed these steps (see Table S1):

Initial conditions: 10% B for 0.25 minutes

Ramp to 80% B over 3 minutes

Increase to 90% B by 4 minutes

Reset to 10% B at 4.1 minutes

Hold at 10% B until method completion at 8 minutes

For pesticide extraction and analysis of MTC, CBF, CBR, and DMT, methanol (99% purity, 

Merck)  and  deionized  water  were  used  as  solvents.  These  conditions  ensured  optimal 

separation and precise quantification of the analytes.

 Mass Spectrometry Conditions

Mass  spectrometric  analysis  was  performed  in  positive  electron  ionization  (ESI)  mode, 

employing  Multiple  Reaction  Monitoring  (MRM)  for  the  targeted  detection  of  the  pesticide 

compounds. The key operating parameters were as follows:

Capillary voltage: 3 kV

Desolvation temperature: 500°C

Desolvation gas flow: 1000 L/h

Cone gas flow: 10 L/h

The  specific  MS/MS  parameters  for  DMT  are  detailed  in  Table  S2.  These  optimized 

conditions provided enhanced sensitivity and precision in the detection of the analytes.

 S3. Photolysis and photocatalysis degradation methylene blue (MB) by TNWs/TNAs and 

Au–TNWs/TNAs

Figure S2. (a, b, c) The time-dependent absorption spectra of MB under UV-Vis irradiation 

during photolysis and photocatalysis using TNWs/TNAs and Au–TNWs/TNAs.

Figure  S3.  (a,  b,  c,  d)  Changes  in  the  absorption  spectra  of  MB  under  UV-Vis  irradiation 

during photolysis and photocatalysis using Au-TNWs/TNAs over four recycling cycles.

The abrupt reduction in absorbance around 600 nm is observed in all spectra. This feature 

is not related to the chemical nature of methylene blue (MB) or the formation of degradation 

intermediates,  as  it  also  appears  in  the  initial  MB  solution.  Instead,  it  arises  from  an 

instrumentation  artifact  of  our  UV–Vis  spectrophotometer,  which  employs  a  diffraction 

grating and order-sorting filters. In aging instruments, filter switching near ~590–610 nm can 

cause a temporary mismatch between the sample and reference beams, producing a sharp dip 

 in  the  spectrum.  Importantly,  this  artifact  does  not  interfere  with  the  characteristic  MB 

absorption band at 650–664 nm, which was used to evaluate photocatalytic degradation. Thus, 

the accuracy of the results and the conclusions of this work are not affected. 

S4.  MRM  chromatogram  of  methiocarb  (MTC),  carbofuran  (CBF),  carbaryl  (CBR), 

and dimethoate (DMT) by photocatalysics (Au-TNWs/TNAs)

Overall,  after  photocatalysis  processes  using  Au-TNWs/TNAs,  the  intensities  of  the  MRM 

peaks  gradually  decreased  over  time,  indicating  a  reduction  in  the  concentrations  of 

methiocarb (MTC), carbofuran (CBF), carbaryl (CBR), and dimethoate (DMT).
